q: 'Canadians are really nice people. Therefore Derek, who is from Vancouver, must be really nice.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A trait of the group (Canadians) is assumed for one member (Derek). It runs from group to individual, so it is not hasty generalisation. This is the lecture's example.

q: In the lecture, Prof. Muratov said that reasoning 'there are many criminals from Russia, so Russians must be bad people' commits which fallacy?
why: He used national stereotypes like this to illustrate division. Strictly, division runs from the whole group to a member (like the Derek example); reasoning from some members to the whole group is closer to hasty generalisation.

q: 'Inha University in Tashkent is one of the best universities in the country, so every professor who works there must be excellent.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A quality of the whole institution is assumed for each member. That is division, not a generalisation from a small sample.

q: A tourist says: 'Uzbeks are famous for their hospitality, so the taxi driver picking me up at the airport will surely invite me home for plov.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A trait of the nation as a whole is assumed for one particular person.

q: 'Real Madrid is the strongest football team in Spain, so each of its players must be the best in Spain at his position.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The team's strength as a whole is assumed to belong to each individual player.

q: What is the key difference between the fallacy of division and hasty generalisation?
choices: Division goes from the whole group to a member; hasty generalisation goes from a few cases to the whole group
Division goes from a few cases to the whole group; hasty generalisation goes from the whole group to a member
Division is a formal fallacy, while hasty generalisation is an informal fallacy
Division concerns emotional appeals, while hasty generalisation concerns word meanings
why: Think of direction: division is group to individual (Canadians to Derek); hasty generalisation is a few individuals to the group (a few abusive men to all men).

q: Which fallacy occurs when, instead of offering a counterargument, we attack the character of the person who made the argument?
why: Ad hominem targets the person. A straw man targets a distorted version of their argument.

q: What is a personal attack (ad hominem) fallacy?
choices: Rejecting an argument by attacking the person who made it
Misrepresenting the opponent's argument to knock it down
Threatening the opponent so that they back down from their view
Changing the subject to avoid answering a hard question
why: Ad hominem tries to create disapproval of the person instead of answering the argument. The others are straw man, appeal to force and red herring.

q: Personal attack (ad hominem) belongs to which family?
why: The person's character is logically irrelevant to whether their argument is sound.

q: In a TV debate about a tax plan, a candidate says: 'Why would anyone listen to my opponent on taxes? He's been divorced twice and failed at running his own business.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The opponent's private life is attacked instead of his tax plan. His argument isn't restated or distorted, so it's not a straw man.

q: A blogger posts a detailed argument for more bike lanes in Tashkent. The top comment says: 'Who cares what you think? You're 19 and still live with your parents.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The commenter attacks the blogger's age and situation instead of the argument. The lecture mentions comment sections as a typical place for this.

q: In a group project meeting, Sardor says: 'Let's ignore Malika's idea for the presentation. She's always late to class anyway.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Being late says nothing about whether her idea is good. Her character is attacked in place of her idea.

q: 'Of course the professor wants a longer semester. He's just a boring old man with no life outside the university.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The professor is insulted rather than his reasons for a longer semester being answered.

q: In a class debate, every time her opponent speaks, Nodira rolls her eyes and smirks at the audience instead of responding to his points. Which fallacy is she committing without words?
why: The lecture notes that personal attacks (and appeals to force) can be non-verbal: eye-rolling, glaring, looking or walking away. She belittles the person instead of answering.

q: The strategy 'don't confuse the soundness of an argument with the character or circumstances of the person making it' mainly protects you against which fallacy?
why: Judging an argument by the person who makes it is exactly what ad hominem does.

q: Which fallacy uses, or threatens to use, physical, psychological or legal force to make someone accept a conclusion or back down?
why: Threats in place of reasons are an appeal to force. The lecture stresses that the force can be physical, psychological or legal.

q: What is an appeal to force (scare tactics)?
choices: Using threats or fear to get someone to accept a conclusion
Evoking sympathy when sympathy is irrelevant to the point
Predicting that one small step will lead to disaster down the line
Attacking the character of the person who is arguing
why: Appeal to force is about threats and fear. Predicting disaster from one small step is slippery slope.

q: Appeal to force (scare tactics) belongs to which family?
why: A threat is logically irrelevant to whether the conclusion is true, but it feels persuasive.

q: A father tells his daughter: 'You don't get to disagree with me while I'm paying your university tuition and putting a roof over your head.' Which fallacy is this?
why: This is the lecture's own example: an implied threat (losing tuition and housing) shuts down disagreement instead of giving a reason why he's right.

q: A restaurant owner messages a customer: 'Delete your negative Google Maps review, or our lawyers will sue you for defamation.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A legal threat is used to make the customer back down. The lecture counts legal force alongside physical and psychological force.

q: At a meeting, the boss says: 'Anyone who thinks the new overtime policy is unfair can explain that at their contract renewal.' Which fallacy is this?
why: It's a veiled threat to people's jobs, used instead of a reason why the policy is fair. The lecture names employers among those who use this tactic.

q: A bigger student leans over a classmate's desk, cracks his knuckles and says: 'You'll agree my answer is right, if you know what's good for you.' Which fallacy is this?
why: An implied physical threat replaces any reason the answer is right. He isn't attacking the classmate's character, so it's not ad hominem.

q: The lecture uses AI company CEOs, who warn that AI could doom humanity within a decade, as an example of which fallacy?
why: He presents the doom predictions of figures like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei as scare tactics: fear is used to win acceptance of a conclusion.

q: After describing AI CEOs' doom predictions, what did the lecturer ask students to do?
choices: Ask whether to believe them, and why the CEOs make such claims
Accept the predictions, since the CEOs are experts in their own field
Dismiss the claims outright, because the CEOs personally profit from AI
Find out how many people agree with the predictions
why: He wanted critical reflection on motive and evidence. Dismissing the claims just because of who makes them would itself be an ad hominem.

q: A senior manager says nothing, but stands over a junior colleague's desk and glares at her until she withdraws her objection to his plan. Which fallacy is conveyed through his body language?
why: The lecture notes that appeals to force can be non-verbal, such as glaring. Intimidation, not reasons, makes her back down.

q: Which fallacy evokes pity in another person when pity is irrelevant to the conclusion?
why: That is the definition of appeal to pity. The key word is irrelevant.

q: What is an appeal to pity?
choices: Trying to win agreement by evoking sympathy that's irrelevant to the point
Trying to win agreement by threatening the other person with consequences
Trying to win agreement by pointing out that almost everyone already agrees
Trying to win agreement by citing an expert from a completely different field
why: Appeal to pity uses irrelevant sympathy. The others describe appeal to force, popular appeal and inappropriate appeal to authority.

q: Appeal to pity belongs to which family?
why: Pity that has nothing to do with the conclusion is logically irrelevant, yet emotionally powerful.

q: Stopped for speeding, a driver tells the police officer: 'Please understand, something terrible just happened at home and I'm not in a good state.' According to the lecture, which fallacy is this?
why: The driver tries to evoke the officer's sympathy, which is irrelevant to whether he was speeding. This is the lecture's example.

q: A student emails the professor: 'Please change my F to a B. My family has had a hard year, and my father will be so disappointed.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The family's hardship may be real, but it is irrelevant to what grade the work deserves.

q: A job applicant says: 'You should hire me rather than the more qualified candidates. I've been unemployed for six months and my rent is due.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Sympathy for his situation doesn't show he is the best person for the job.

q: At Chorsu Bazaar, a seller insists: 'This melon is worth 60,000 som. I've been standing in the heat since 5 a.m. and my kids need new shoes.' Which fallacy is he using?
why: His hard day doesn't make the melon worth more. He uses sympathy instead of reasons about the melon.

q: A defence lawyer argues: 'My client could not have stolen the car. Just look at how much he has suffered since childhood.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A hard childhood is irrelevant to whether he stole the car. This isn't the court exception to appeal to ignorance either, since nothing is said about proof.

q: When is appealing to someone's pity NOT a fallacy?
choices: When pity is relevant to the conclusion, as in a flood-relief appeal
When the person telling the sad story is being completely honest about it
When the listener ends up agreeing with the speaker's conclusion anyway
When the appeal is made in a formal setting such as a court
why: By definition the fallacy is evoking pity when it's irrelevant. A true sad story is still fallacious if it doesn't bear on the conclusion, like the speeding driver's.

q: Which fallacy appeals to popular opinion to gain support for a conclusion?
why: Popular appeal relies on what the crowd thinks. Its main forms are the bandwagon and snob appeal.

q: What is the fallacy of popular appeal?
choices: Treating a conclusion as true because many people believe it or do it
Treating a conclusion as true because an expert in another field says so
Treating a conclusion as true because no one has proven it false
Treating a conclusion as true because a small sample supports it
why: Popularity isn't evidence. The other options describe inappropriate appeal to authority, appeal to ignorance and hasty generalisation.

q: Popular appeal (bandwagon, snob appeal) belongs to which family?
why: How many people believe something is logically irrelevant to whether it is true.

q: What is the bandwagon approach, the most common form of popular appeal?
choices: Assuming a conclusion is true simply because everyone believes it or does it
Linking a product to admired celebrities so that people want to be like them
Assuming that once one step is allowed, everything else will follow
Quoting a famous person on a topic as if they were an expert in it
why: Bandwagon means 'everyone's doing it, so it must be right'. Linking products to celebrities is snob appeal, the other form the lecture mentions.

q: In the lecture, what is snob appeal?
choices: Popular appeal using footballers or celebrities to make you want a product
A personal attack that mocks people from a lower social class or with less income
An appeal to force in which wealthy, powerful people threaten poorer people
An equivocation in which luxury words quietly change their meaning
why: The lecture treats snob appeal as a form of popular appeal: you are meant to want the product because admired people have it.

q: 'God must exist. After all, most people believe in God.' Which fallacy does the lecture say this is?
why: Bandwagon: God's existence doesn't depend on how many people believe. It's not appeal to ignorance, since nothing is said about a lack of proof.

q: 'Everyone in our group uses ChatGPT to write their essays, so it must be fine.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Bandwagon: 'everyone is doing it' is offered as the reason it's acceptable.

q: A TV ad shows a famous Uzbek national-team footballer drinking a soda, with the slogan 'Drink what champions drink.' According to the lecture, which fallacy is the ad using?
why: The lecture's example of snob appeal, a type of popular appeal: footballers and celebrities advertising products so you'll want what they have.

q: 'All the top students at the presidential school wear this watch brand. Buy one and join the elite.' Which fallacy is the ad using?
why: Snob appeal: the product is sold through association with an admired, elite group.

q: 'Ten million people downloaded this messaging app this month, so it must be the safest one to use.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Bandwagon: popularity is treated as proof of safety.

q: What separates snob appeal from an inappropriate appeal to authority?
choices: Snob appeal sells through admired people; inappropriate authority uses an expert outside their field
Snob appeal uses an expert outside their field; inappropriate authority sells through admired people
Snob appeal is a fallacy of ambiguity; inappropriate authority is a fallacy of relevance
Snob appeal relies on threats; inappropriate authority relies on evoking pity
why: Snob appeal (a relevance fallacy) says 'want it because admired people have it'. Inappropriate appeal to authority (an unwarranted assumption) takes someone's word on a subject outside their expertise.

q: Which fallacy claims something is true because no one has proven it false, or false because no one has proven it true?
why: Treating a lack of proof as proof of the opposite is appeal to ignorance.

q: What is an appeal to ignorance?
choices: Taking a lack of proof as proof of the opposite
Dismissing an argument because the person making it is uneducated
Ignoring the opponent's argument and changing the subject instead
Relying on what most uninformed people happen to believe
why: It is about absence of proof. Calling the arguer uneducated would be a personal attack.

q: Appeal to ignorance belongs to which family?
why: It can sound like an unwarranted assumption, but the lecture lists it under relevance: a lack of proof is irrelevant to whether a claim is true.

q: In 'appeal to ignorance', what does 'ignorance' mean?
choices: Lacking the means to prove or disprove something
Being stupid, uneducated or poorly informed in general
Ignoring what the other person is actually saying
Not knowing what the majority of people think
why: The lecture is explicit: it does not mean we are stupid. It means we don't have the means of proving or disproving the claim.

q: What important exception to the appeal-to-ignorance fallacy does the lecture mention?
choices: In court, a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty
In science, a theory is accepted until someone disproves it
In religion, beliefs need no proof of any kind
In advertising, claims are true until a regulator rejects them
why: In law, 'not proven guilty' legitimately means treated as innocent, because the burden of proof is on the prosecution.

q: In a court of law, according to the lecture, who carries the burden of proof?
why: The defendant is presumed innocent, and it is the prosecution that must prove guilt. That is why the court case is an exception to appeal to ignorance.

q: A juror says: 'The prosecution never proved he was at the crime scene, so we have to find him not guilty.' Is this an appeal to ignorance?
choices: No: in court, innocence is presumed and the prosecution must prove guilt
Yes: a lack of proof of guilt doesn't show that he is actually innocent
No, because a juror's reasoning counts as an appeal to expert authority
Yes, because jurors must convict unless the defendant proves his own innocence
why: This is exactly the court exception. Outside a courtroom, 'not proven, so false' would be an appeal to ignorance.

q: 'UFOs don't exist, as no one has been able to prove that they do.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The lecture's example: no proof that UFOs exist doesn't prove they don't. We simply don't know.

q: 'No scientist has ever proven that 5G towers are completely safe, so they must be harmful.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A lack of proof of safety is treated as proof of harm.

q: Your roommate says: 'You can't prove I ate your samsa, so I didn't eat it.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A lack of proof that he ate it doesn't show he didn't. This is a dorm room, not a courtroom, so the legal exception doesn't apply.

q: 'There's no evidence that this new energy drink is harmful, so it's definitely safe for children.' Which fallacy is this?
why: No evidence of harm is treated as proof of safety. It may simply not have been tested.

q: Which fallacy draws a generalisation from a sample that is too small or biased?
why: Small or biased sample, sweeping conclusion: hasty generalisation. Division goes from the group to a member instead.

q: What is a hasty generalisation?
choices: Generalising about a group from a sample that is too small or biased
Assuming each member of a group has the traits of the group as a whole
Assuming that because one event came first, it caused the second
Concluding something is true because most people believe it
why: Hasty generalisation is a few cases stretched to the group. The second option is division, the reverse direction.

q: Hasty generalisation belongs to which family?
why: In this lecture it is a fallacy of relevance. Don't mix it up with division, which is a fallacy of ambiguity.

q: What does the lecture say about generalisation in general?
choices: Used properly, it's a valuable tool in the physical and social sciences
Any generalisation about a group of people is automatically a fallacy
A generalisation is only valid when everyone agrees with it
Generalising is a formal fallacy rather than an informal one, so avoid it
why: Generalising is fine and useful. It only becomes a fallacy when the sample is too small or biased.

q: A woman whose father and brothers were abusive concludes that all men are abusers. According to the lecture, which fallacy is this?
why: A few personal cases (a small, biased sample) are stretched to cover all men. Division would go the other way, from a group trait to one member.

q: After the 9/11 attacks, some people treated all Muslims as potential terrorists. Which fallacy does the lecture say this scapegoating involves?
why: The actions of a few were generalised to a whole religious group. This is the lecture's example.

q: 'I had two rude taxi drivers this week, so all taxi drivers in Tashkent are rude.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Two drivers is far too small a sample to judge thousands.

q: 'I asked five friends in my dorm, and all of them prefer Python to Java. So Inha students prefer Python.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Five friends from one dorm is a small and probably biased sample of the whole student body.

q: A YouTuber polls her own subscribers, finds that 95% love her videos, and announces that the whole country loves her content. Which fallacy is this?
why: Her subscribers are a biased sample: people who already like her. The lecture's definition covers samples that are too small or biased.

q: Which fallacy distorts or misrepresents an opponent's argument to make it easier to refute?
why: Straw man: build a weaker copy of the argument, then knock it down. A red herring changes the subject instead.

q: What is a straw man fallacy?
choices: Attacking a distorted version of the opponent's argument
Changing the subject to a different issue to escape the original argument
Attacking the opponent's character instead of the argument they made
Using one weak example to make a generalisation about everyone
why: The straw man is the distorted version of the argument. The other options describe red herring, ad hominem and hasty generalisation.

q: The straw man fallacy belongs to which family?
why: Refuting a distorted version is irrelevant to whether the real argument holds.

q: 'Mamdani wants free public transport and to tax the rich. He supports socialism. But socialism was already tried and failed in the Soviet Union. Therefore his argument is invalid.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Specific proposals (free transit, taxing the rich) are recast as 'Soviet socialism', a distorted version that's easier to knock down. This is the lecture's own example.

q: The student council proposes allowing laptops in open-book exams. An opponent replies: 'So basically they want exams with no rules at all, where anyone can cheat.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A limited proposal (laptops in open-book exams) is recast as 'no rules at all', which is easy to reject. The topic hasn't changed, so it's not a red herring.

q: Wife: 'I think we should eat out a bit less this month.' Husband: 'So you want us to never have fun again and sit at home eating plain bread?' Which fallacy is the husband committing?
why: He exaggerates 'eat out a bit less' into 'never have fun again', which is easier to attack.

q: City planners propose limiting cars in the historic centre on weekends. A critic posts: 'The planners want to ban all cars and force everyone to walk to work in the middle of winter!' Which fallacy is this?
why: A weekend limit in one area becomes a total ban on cars, a misrepresentation built to be knocked down.

q: A student argues that evolution should be taught in school. His opponent replies: 'He thinks your grandmother was a monkey at the zoo. Nobody sane believes that.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The theory of evolution is caricatured into something absurd, then rejected. The opponent stays on topic, so it's not a red herring.

q: According to the lecture, how do you avoid committing or falling for a straw man?
choices: Recheck the original argument for distortions or omissions
Define all of the ambiguous terms before the discussion begins in earnest
Ask whether there are more than the two options being offered
Check whether the person making the argument has a good character
why: Ask: has the argument been reworded or oversimplified to the point of misrepresentation? Have key parts been omitted or key words changed?

q: What is the difference between a straw man and a red herring?
choices: A straw man attacks a distorted version of the argument; a red herring changes the subject to another issue
A straw man changes the subject to another issue; a red herring attacks a distorted version of the argument
A straw man attacks the person's character; a red herring attacks the person's family or friends
A straw man is a fallacy of relevance; a red herring is a fallacy of ambiguity
why: Both are fallacies of relevance. The straw man stays on topic but distorts it; the red herring leaves the topic.

q: Which fallacy tries to sidetrack an argument by going off on a tangent and raising a different issue?
why: Sidetracking to a different issue is a red herring. A straw man stays on the issue but distorts it.

q: According to the slides, what is a red herring?
choices: A response aimed at a different conclusion from the original argument's
A response that restates the original conclusion in slightly different words
A response that attacks the character of the person who made the argument
A response that exaggerates the original argument so it is easy to defeat
why: A red herring answers a different question. Exaggerating the argument is a straw man; restating the conclusion is begging the question.

q: The red herring belongs to which family?
why: The new issue is logically irrelevant to the original conclusion.

q: 'Why are you upset about my driving after a few drinks? It's not a big deal. Look at all the accidents caused by people talking on their phones.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Instead of defending drink-driving, the speaker drags attention to phone use, a different issue. Nobody's argument is distorted, so it's not a straw man. This is the lecture's example.

q: A journalist asks a minister why electricity prices rose 30% this year. The minister replies: 'Let's not forget that our country just hosted a hugely successful international summit.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The minister dodges a hard question by bringing up an unrelated success. The lecture notes this is common in politics.

q: Caught copying an essay, a student tells the dean: 'Why focus on me? The cafeteria food here is terrible and nobody does anything about that.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Cafeteria food has nothing to do with plagiarism. He is changing the subject.

q: Parent: 'Why did you get a C in calculus?' Teenager: 'Did you know Aziz's parents just bought him a new iPhone?' Which fallacy is the teenager using?
why: The teenager throws the conversation off the scent of the grade.

q: Where does the name 'red herring' come from, according to the lecture?
choices: UK fox hunting: a smelly fish was used to throw hounds off the scent
Norwegian fish markets, where cheap fish were dyed red to fool the buyers
A British navy code name for a decoy ship sent to mislead enemy fleets
A Russian folk tale about a fish that tricked a hungry bear
why: With fox hounds, a strong-smelling herring was used to pull the dogs' attention away from the real trail. The fallacy pulls an argument away from the real issue.

q: In which fallacy is the conclusion simply a rewording of a premise?
why: Restating the premise as the conclusion is begging the question. A loaded question hides an assumption inside a question.

q: What is begging the question?
choices: Assuming the conclusion is true by making it the same as a premise
Asking a question that presumes the answer to an unasked question
Asking so many questions that the opponent eventually gives up
Reducing a complex issue to just two possible choices for the listener
why: Despite the name, it has nothing to do with asking questions. A question that presumes an answer is a loaded question.

q: Begging the question is also known as...
why: The argument goes in a circle: the conclusion is used to support itself. Post hoc is questionable cause; either/or is false dilemma.

q: Begging the question belongs to which family?
why: It assumes the very conclusion it should be proving, which is an unsupported assumption.

q: 'Capital punishment is wrong because it is immoral to inflict death as a punishment for a crime.' Which fallacy is this?
why: 'Immoral to inflict death as punishment' just restates 'capital punishment is wrong'. It defines the key term rather than giving a reason. This is the lecture's example.

q: 'Smoking is unhealthy because it is bad for your health.' Which fallacy is this?
why: 'Unhealthy' and 'bad for your health' mean the same thing. The premise is the conclusion in different words.

q: 'Our university's attendance rules are fair because they are just.' Which fallacy is this?
why: 'Fair' and 'just' are synonyms here, so no independent reason is given. The meaning doesn't shift, so it isn't equivocation.

q: 'Rustam is the best candidate for class president, because none of the other candidates is as good as he is.' Which fallacy is this?
why: 'Best candidate' and 'no one else is as good' say the same thing. It's a circle, not a reason.

q: 'This news channel always tells the truth. I know because the channel itself says it is the most truthful source in the country.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The channel's honesty is proven by trusting the channel, which assumes what it set out to prove. That's circular reasoning.

q: Why does the lecture say begging the question can be hard to spot?
choices: It seems logical until you notice premise and conclusion say the same
It is always hidden inside a question rather than stated openly as a claim
It relies on stressing one word in a way that listeners easily miss
It only ever appears in written texts and never in spoken arguments
why: At first glance there seems to be a logical argument. On closer evaluation the premise and the conclusion say essentially the same thing.

q: How does begging the question differ from a loaded question?
choices: Begging the question restates its premise as its conclusion; a loaded question hides an assumption inside a question
Begging the question hides an assumption inside a question; a loaded question restates its premise as its conclusion
Begging the question is a fallacy of relevance; a loaded question is a fallacy of ambiguity
Begging the question attacks the person; a loaded question attacks the person's argument
why: Both belong to the unwarranted assumptions family, which is why they are easy to mix up. Only the loaded question is actually a question.

q: Which fallacy looks to an authority in a field other than the one under investigation?
why: Citing an expert is fine when they are an expert on this topic. Citing them on a different field is the fallacy.

q: What is an inappropriate appeal to authority?
choices: Relying on an expert from the wrong field
Rejecting an expert's view because of the expert's personal life or past
Assuming something is true because the majority believes it
Using a powerful person's threat to force someone to agree
why: The fault is borrowing authority from the wrong field. Rejecting an expert over their private life would be ad hominem.

q: Inappropriate appeal to authority belongs to which family?
why: It assumes, without evidence, that expertise in one field carries over to another.

q: According to the lecture, when is it appropriate to use the testimony of an authority?
choices: When the person is an expert in the very field under discussion
When the person is famous and widely trusted by the public
When the person holds a high position in the government or ministry
When the person has a very large following on social media
why: Testimony from a genuine expert in the field is generally appropriate. Fame, rank or followers don't make someone an authority on the topic.

q: A popular lifestyle blogger is invited onto a podcast as 'today's expert' and explains how the national economy should be managed. Listeners treat her advice as authoritative. Which fallacy is this?
why: The lecture specifically mentions celebrities and bloggers given the microphone on podcasts to talk about politics, family or money, outside their field.

q: 'A Nobel Prize-winning physicist said in an interview that this diet cures diabetes, so it must work.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A physicist is a real expert, but in physics, not medicine or nutrition.

q: In a debate about computer graphics, a student argues: 'My uncle is a senior network engineer, and he says ray tracing is a dead end, so it must be.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The lecture warns that IT has many sub-fields. Expertise in networking doesn't make someone an authority on graphics rendering.

q: A famous actor tells viewers which presidential candidate has the best foreign policy, and the TV host adds: 'Who would know better than him?' Which fallacy is this?
why: Acting fame is treated as expertise in foreign policy. The host explicitly frames him as an authority.

q: 'A world chess champion says vaccines weaken the immune system, and he's a genius, so we shouldn't vaccinate our kids.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Brilliance at chess gives no authority on immunology.

q: Which fallacy presumes a particular answer to another, unasked question?
why: A loaded question carries a hidden assumption. Begging the question restates the premise as the conclusion.

q: What is a loaded question?
choices: A question that already assumes the answer to a question nobody asked
An argument whose conclusion just repeats one of its premises
A question that offers only two answers to a complex issue
A question asked to move the discussion away from the real issue at hand
why: The hidden, unasked question is the trap. Offering only two options is false dilemma.

q: The loaded question belongs to which family?
why: The question rests on an unsupported assumption (e.g. that you did beat your wife).

q: In court, a lawyer demands: 'Have you stopped beating your wife? Answer yes or no.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Either answer admits he has beaten her. The question presumes the answer to the unasked question 'Did you ever beat her?'. This is the lecture's example.

q: A journalist asks the minister: 'When will you stop lying to the public about the budget?' Which fallacy is this?
why: The question assumes, without evidence, that the minister has been lying.

q: With no evidence, a teacher asks a student: 'Why did you copy your essay from the internet?' Which fallacy is this?
why: It presumes the answer to the unasked question 'Did you copy it?'.

q: A mother asks her son: 'Are you still wasting all your time on video games?' Which fallacy is this?
why: Answering yes or no both admit he was wasting all his time. The yes/no format isn't what makes it a false dilemma; the hidden assumption is the problem.

q: A survey asks residents: 'How much has the mayor's corruption harmed your mahalla?' Which fallacy is built into the question?
why: The question assumes the mayor is corrupt, which nobody has established.

q: What distinguishes a loaded question from a false dilemma?
choices: A loaded question smuggles in an unproven assumption; a false dilemma squeezes a complex issue into two options
A loaded question squeezes a complex issue into two options; a false dilemma smuggles in an unproven assumption
A loaded question is a fallacy of relevance; a false dilemma is a fallacy of ambiguity
A loaded question is only used in courts; a false dilemma is only used in politics
why: Both are unwarranted assumptions. 'Have you stopped beating your wife?' is loaded because of what it presumes, not because it demands yes or no.

q: Which fallacy reduces the responses to a complex issue to an either/or choice?
why: Either/or thinking on a complex issue is a false dilemma.

q: What is a false dilemma?
choices: Presenting only two options when more exist
Predicting that one step will lead to extremes
Assuming the answer to an unasked question
Distorting the opponent's view to defeat it
why: A false dilemma hides the other options. The rest describe slippery slope, loaded question and straw man.

q: The false dilemma belongs to which family?
why: It assumes, without evidence, that only two options exist.

q: According to the lecture, what does a false dilemma do to a debate?
choices: It polarises positions and ignores common ground or other solutions
It makes the key terms shift their meaning partway through the debate
It forces the debate back to the original argument
It replaces real evidence with appeals to what most people think is true
why: By offering only two sides, it pushes people to extremes and hides compromise or third options.

q: 'Why do you complain about our politics? If you don't like our policies, you can leave the country.' Which fallacy is this?
why: It offers only two choices, accept everything or leave, and ignores voting, debate or reform. This is the lecture's example.

q: 'Either you support every decision the dean makes, or you're against this university.' Which fallacy is this?
why: You can support the university and still disagree with some decisions. Those middle positions are ignored.

q: 'Either we build a highway through the city park, or traffic in Tashkent will never improve.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Metro lines, buses, bike lanes and congestion pricing are all ignored. Only two options are offered.

q: A father tells his daughter: 'You either get into medical school or you'll be a failure in life.' Which fallacy is this?
why: There are countless successful paths besides medicine. The father reduces them to two.

q: 'Either you post about this cause on Instagram, or you clearly don't care about it at all.' Which fallacy is this?
why: People can care by donating, volunteering or acting offline. Those options are left out.

q: Which fallacy assumes, without sufficient evidence, that one thing is the cause of another?
why: An unsupported causal claim is questionable cause, also called post hoc.

q: What is the fallacy of questionable cause?
choices: Assuming without evidence that one thing caused another
Assuming that allowing one action will lead to all its extreme forms
Assuming that something natural must be good or acceptable
Assuming that a group's traits belong to each of its members
why: Questionable cause is about unsupported causal links. The others are slippery slope, naturalistic fallacy and division.

q: Questionable cause (post hoc) belongs to which family?
why: It assumes a causal link that no evidence supports.

q: What is the 'post hoc' form of questionable cause?
choices: Assuming that because one event came before another, it caused it
Assuming that because something is natural, it is morally good
Assuming that because no one disproved a claim, it must therefore be true
Assuming that because a few cases agree, all cases will agree
why: Post hoc is short for 'after this, therefore because of this'. Coming first doesn't make something a cause.

q: Which principle does the lecture use to sum up the problem with questionable cause?
choices: Correlation does not always mean causation
Absence of evidence is evidence of absence
why: Two things happening together, or one after the other, doesn't prove one caused the other. The second option is itself the appeal-to-ignorance mistake.

q: Why are we prone to questionable cause, according to the lecture?
choices: Our brains tend to impose order, so we see causal links that aren't there
We trust experts too much, even when they speak well outside their own fields
We are afraid of being left out of what the majority of our friends believe
We don't define our key terms clearly before starting to argue
why: Our brains impose order on how we see the world, so we see causes where none exist. Superstitions are the classic result.

q: 'I wore my lucky jacket to the exam and got an A, so I'll wear it to every exam from now on.' According to the lecture, this superstition is an example of which fallacy?
why: Wearing the jacket came before the A, so it's assumed to have caused it. The lecture uses the lucky jacket and the lucky route to the exam as examples.

q: Classmates avoid sitting near a student with a skin condition that isn't contagious, assuming they'll catch it if they get close. Which fallacy does the lecture link this to?
why: They assume, without evidence, that being near her will cause them to get the condition. The lecture blames unfamiliarity with the condition.

q: 'Ever since the new rector arrived, our university football team keeps winning. He must be the reason.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The wins came after his arrival, but nothing shows he caused them (post hoc).

q: 'Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer, so eating ice cream causes drowning.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Correlation isn't causation. Hot weather drives both.

q: 'I drank green tea with lemon, and the next morning my cold was gone. So green tea cures colds.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Colds go away on their own. The tea came first, so it's assumed to be the cause.

q: What is the difference between questionable cause and slippery slope?
choices: Questionable cause asserts an unproven causal link; slippery slope says allowing one step leads to the extremes
Questionable cause says allowing one step leads to the extremes; slippery slope asserts an unproven causal link
Questionable cause is a fallacy of relevance; slippery slope is a fallacy of ambiguity
Questionable cause concerns only past events; slippery slope concerns only natural events
why: Both involve causes, which is why they get confused. Slippery slope is specifically about permitting one action and predicting a chain to its most extreme form.

q: Which fallacy assumes that if a certain action is permitted, then all actions of this type, even the most extreme, will soon be permissible?
why: Allow one thing and everything follows: that's slippery slope.

q: What is a slippery slope fallacy?
choices: Claiming one allowed step will lead to the extremes
Claiming that one event caused another because it happened first
Claiming that only two options are available on a complex, many-sided issue
Claiming that one bad case proves that a whole group is bad
why: The slope is the imagined chain from a small step to the extreme. The others describe questionable cause, false dilemma and hasty generalisation.

q: The slippery slope belongs to which family?
why: It assumes, without evidence, that one small step will lead all the way to the extreme.

q: A neighbour warns: 'If you let your son skip one family dinner to play football, next he'll skip school, and he'll end up a criminal.' Which fallacy is this?
why: One small permission is said to lead to the most extreme result. The lecture uses parenting examples like this.

q: 'If we listen to the students' complaints about the dormitory just once, tomorrow they'll take over the whole university and go on strike.' Which fallacy is this?
why: This mirrors the lecture's example about giving young people a voice 'just once'. A single concession is assumed to snowball.

q: 'If the police let drivers go 10 km/h over the limit, soon nobody in the city will obey any traffic law at all.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A small tolerance is assumed to lead to total lawlessness, with no evidence for the chain.

q: 'If we let one employee work from home on Fridays, soon everyone will stay home all week and the company will collapse.' Which fallacy is this?
why: One permission is assumed to lead straight to the most extreme outcome.

q: A professor refuses a quiz retake: 'If I let you retake this quiz, next you'll demand to retake every exam, and grades will mean nothing.' Which fallacy is this?
why: There may be good reasons to refuse, but this one assumes an unproven chain from one retake to meaningless grades.

q: Which fallacy rests on the assumption that what is natural is good or morally acceptable, and what is unnatural is bad?
why: Natural = good, unnatural = bad is the naturalistic fallacy.

q: What is the naturalistic fallacy?
choices: Assuming that what is natural is good and what is unnatural is bad
Assuming that a cause must naturally come before its effect
Assuming that natural scientists are experts on every topic
Assuming that the traits of nature must apply to every single living thing
why: It is the unwarranted jump from 'natural' to 'good' (or 'unnatural' to 'bad').

q: The naturalistic fallacy belongs to which family?
why: It rests on the unwarranted assumption that natural means good.

q: Which counterexamples did the lecture give to show that 'natural' doesn't always mean 'good'?
why: Tobacco is natural yet harmful; hurricanes and earthquakes are natural yet dangerous. Fruit and vegetables were his examples of natural things that usually are good.

q: 'Predators hunt other animals in nature, and humans are predators too, so hunting rare animals is perfectly acceptable.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Hunting being natural is taken to make it morally fine, even for rare species. This is the lecture's example.

q: 'This herbal supplement is 100% natural, so it can't have any harmful side effects.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Natural doesn't mean safe. Tobacco and poisonous plants are natural too.

q: 'Vaccines are made of artificial chemicals, so they must be bad for children.' Which fallacy is this?
why: This is the reverse form: unnatural is assumed to be bad.

q: 'It's natural for people to get angry, so shouting at your colleagues is morally fine.' Which fallacy is this?
why: That anger is natural doesn't make acting on it acceptable.

q: 'Mushrooms grow wild in nature, so any mushroom you find in the forest is safe to eat.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Being natural is taken as proof of being good or safe, yet many wild mushrooms are poisonous.

q: Which of these is one of the lecture's nine strategies for avoiding fallacies?
choices: Always side with the majority view
why: 'Don't be set on winning' is strategy nine. The others would push you into popular appeal or inappropriate appeal to authority.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the nine strategies for avoiding fallacies?
choices: Rely on popular opinion to settle disagreements
Do not confuse the soundness of an argument with the character of the person making it
Avoid ambiguous and vague terms and faulty grammar
why: Relying on popular opinion is the popular appeal fallacy. The other three are on the lecture's list.

q: What does the strategy 'know yourself' mean in this lecture?
choices: Learn which fallacies you are most likely to fall for or commit
Trust your own views over the views of other people
Research your own background before entering a debate
Only argue about topics drawn from your own experience
why: Self-knowledge of your weak spots makes you less vulnerable to lapses in critical thinking.

q: Why does building self-confidence and self-esteem help you avoid fallacies?
choices: Confident people back down less under fallacies and get less defensive
Confident people don't need to listen to anyone else's arguments
Confident people can win any argument through sheer force of personality
Confident people automatically become experts in the topic
why: Self-confident people are less likely to give in when a fallacy is used on them, or to get defensive and use fallacies on others.

q: The strategy 'cultivate good listening skills' asks you to...
choices: be a respectful listener even when you disagree
listen only to people who are experts in the field
stay silent until the other person runs out of arguments
listen for words you can later use against the speaker
why: Good listening means respecting others' views, including ones you disagree with.

q: The strategy 'avoid ambiguous and vague terms and faulty grammar' is mainly a defence against which family of fallacies?
why: Defining key terms, using grammar carefully and asking when something is unclear targets equivocation, amphiboly, accent and division.

q: What exception did the lecturer mention to 'don't confuse the soundness of an argument with the character of the person making it'?
choices: In criminal investigations, a suspect's past crimes can be relevant
In politics, a candidate's private life is always relevant
In families, parents' views should outweigh their children's
In science, only famous scientists' arguments deserve attention
why: He noted that police investigators may look at a person's criminal history. In general arguments, though, stick to the argument itself.

q: What does the strategy 'know your topic' advise?
choices: Research and investigate before you conclude
Only argue about topics that you formally studied at university
Memorise the names of all the fallacies before any debate
Let the most knowledgeable person in the room decide the issue for everyone
why: Knowing your subject lets you bring real evidence and better examples instead of jumping to conclusions.

q: What does 'adopt a position of scepticism' mean in the lecture?
choices: Stay sceptical yet open-minded, and doubt your own views too
Reject every claim until it has been proven beyond any possible doubt
Doubt everyone else's claims but trust your own carefully formed views
Accept claims from authorities in any field without asking questions
why: Scepticism isn't a closed mind: keep claims open unless clear evidence contradicts them, don't just take people's word, and apply the same doubt to yourself.

q: Why does the lecture include 'watch your body language' as a strategy?
choices: Personal attacks and threats can be non-verbal, e.g. eye-rolling or glaring
Confident posture makes an argument logically stronger and much harder to refute
Body language reliably reveals whether the other person is lying to you
Fallacies of ambiguity are mostly caused by unclear hand gestures
why: Fallacies need not be spoken: rolling your eyes, glaring, looking away or walking away can carry an ad hominem or a threat.

q: According to the lecture, why shouldn't you be set on 'winning' an argument?
choices: Arguing to win, not to find truth, pushes you to fallacies when stuck
Winning arguments damages friendships, and friendships matter more than truth
The person who wins an argument is usually the one committing the fallacies
Arguments can never truly be won, only postponed until a later time
why: If the goal is winning, you're more likely to fall back on fallacies and rhetoric when you can't rationally defend your position.

q: Before a class debate on whether Tashkent should charge drivers to enter the city centre, Jasur spends a week reading studies from other cities. Which strategy is he following?
why: Researching before concluding is 'know your topic'.

q: Aziza notices she always gives in when her older brother raises his voice, so she decides to watch out for appeals to force in their arguments. Which strategy is she using?
why: Identifying which fallacy you personally tend to fall for is 'know yourself'.

q: In a team meeting, Timur realises his plan has a serious flaw, but keeps arguing anyway so he won't lose face in front of his colleagues. Which strategy is he ignoring?
choices: Avoid ambiguous terms and faulty grammar
why: He is arguing to win rather than to find the truth, which is when people start reaching for fallacies.

q: In a group discussion, Laylo stops and asks: 'When you say the plan is cheap, cheap compared to what?' Which strategy is she applying?
choices: Avoid ambiguous terms and faulty grammar
why: 'Cheap' is a vague, relative term. Asking for it to be defined is the strategy against ambiguity.

q: Kamola strongly disagrees with her classmate's view on AI regulation, but she lets him finish, nods, and summarises his point before responding. Which strategy is she showing?
choices: Avoid ambiguous terms and faulty grammar
why: Being a respectful listener even when you disagree is the listening-skills strategy.

q: After reading an article that supports his own opinion, Doston checks its evidence just as carefully as he would for an article he disagreed with. Which strategy is he applying?
why: The lecture's scepticism strategy explicitly includes staying sceptical of your own views.

q: The lecture opens with a Turkish Airlines ad starring Kobe Bryant and Messi. What point does the lecturer use it to make?
choices: Successful ads can drive sales and build followers and brand loyalty
Ads with celebrities are always an appeal to inappropriate authority
Airlines depend on product placement more than any other industry
Ads featuring athletes are mainly aimed at children and teenagers
why: He picked it because it was one of the most-watched ads on YouTube, to show that a successful ad boosts sales and brand loyalty. He doesn't analyse it as a fallacy.

q: According to the lecture, what is the main purpose of a business, the goal that marketing ultimately serves?
choices: Building brand loyalty among young customers
Informing society about new products and services
Creating jobs by outsourcing production to developing countries
why: He starts from the point that businesses chase profit: the margin left after all costs. Brand loyalty, informing customers and outsourcing are means to that end.

q: Why does the lecturer say marketing has become 'the main job' of many big corporations?
choices: Many design and sell products but outsource the manufacturing to countries like Uzbekistan, China or Vietnam
Consumer-protection laws force them to spend most of their budget on advertising instead of production
Customers today ignore product quality and respond only to celebrity endorsements and discounts
Marketing research has become their main product, which they sell on to smaller companies
why: Some big corporations don't even own factories. They design and market, ship production abroad, and in the end it's all about how much they can sell, and for how much.

q: Identifying a target or niche market and finding out whether it matches customer desires (their problems, needs and what drives them) is called:
why: That's the slide's definition of marketing research. A strategic plan comes after the research and decides how to use the company's resources.

q: Which three methods of marketing research does the lecture list?
why: Surveys collect information, observation monitors buying patterns, and experimentation measures cause and effect. Focus groups are a kind of survey, not a separate method.

q: A Korzinka employee stops shoppers at the exit and asks them to rate the new self-checkout machines on a tablet. Which marketing research method is this?
why: Asking people questions to collect information is a survey; in-store and street surveys are his examples. Observation would mean watching what shoppers do without asking them anything.

q: A phone brand invites eight students to a room in Tashkent and asks them, as a group, what they dislike about their current phones. Which marketing research method does this focus group belong to?
choices: Strategic planning (deploying resources to a goal)
why: He lists focus groups under surveys, next to online and in-person questionnaires. The company is asking people, not watching them or testing a change.

q: Uzum Market's data team tracks which ads customers clicked before arriving, what they browsed, and how long they took to decide before buying. Which marketing research method is this?
why: Monitoring buying behaviour and patterns, often through big data and website click paths, is observation. Nobody is asked anything (survey) and nothing is deliberately changed (experimentation).

q: A juice company sells the same juice in two different package designs in two similar Tashkent districts for a month, to see which design sells more. Which marketing research method is this?
why: The company changes one factor (packaging) and measures its effect on buying: a cause-and-effect test. Packaging, delivery and call-centre changes are his examples of experimentation.

q: In marketing research, 'observation' means:
choices: Monitoring customers' buying behaviour and patterns
Asking customers questions online, in shops or in focus groups
Changing one factor, such as packaging, and measuring the effect on sales
Identifying a niche market and checking it against customer desires
why: Observation watches what customers actually do, for example through big data. Asking questions is a survey, and changing a factor to measure its effect is experimentation.

q: In the lecture, a 'strategic plan' is:
choices: A method by which an organization deploys its resources to realize a goal
Identifying a target market and checking whether it matches customer desires
Placing a real product inside a film or sports broadcast so it goes unnoticed
Measuring how a change in packaging or delivery affects customers' buying
why: That's the slide definition. It builds on marketing research (identifying the target market), which comes first and tells the company what customers want.

q: Which three strategies does the lecture give as examples of a company's strategic plan?
choices: Brand recognition, motivating impulse buying, lengthening the purchase experience
Creating product awareness, informing customers about features, motivating demand
why: The other lists are the three research methods, the three purposes of advertising, and a mix of ad types with a fallacy.

q: A fast-food chain invests heavily in a simple logo and signature colours, so that even a small child or an elderly person recognises its restaurants instantly. Which strategy is this?
why: He describes brand recognition as investing in logos, colours, mission statements and so on, so that anyone, even a child, recognises the brand at a glance.

q: Uzum Market shows a banner, 'Flash sale −40%, ends in 09:59', with a countdown timer. Which marketing strategy is this?
why: Discounts, lots of options and a short window to decide are his examples of pushing people to buy without making a conscious decision.

q: In Havas the bread is near the entrance but the checkout is at the far end, so you walk past almost every shelf. How does the lecturer classify this layout?
choices: Lengthening the purchase experience, done on purpose
Motivating impulse buying with discounts and short deadlines
Brand recognition through the store's colours and logo
Observation of customers' buying patterns in the store
why: His Havas/Korzinka 'labyrinth' is the example of lengthening the purchase experience: the longer you stay, the more you're likely to buy. You may grab things on impulse on the way, but the layout itself is about time in the shop.

q: Which three purposes of advertising does the lecture name?
choices: Building brand loyalty, lowering prices, beating competitors
Surveying, observing and experimenting on customers
Entertaining viewers, funding TV channels, sponsoring sports teams
why: These are the slide's three purposes. Surveying, observing and experimenting are marketing research, which happens before advertising.

q: Which purpose of advertising does the lecturer call the main one?
why: He lists it last but calls it the main purpose: in the end, people have to come and buy the product or use the service.

q: A new online bookshop goes live, but nobody visits because nobody knows it exists. Which purpose of advertising does it need to serve first?
why: This is his own example: you make a product, post it on your site, and nobody knows about it. Advertising first makes people aware it exists. The last two are marketing strategies, not ad purposes.

q: A well-known mobile operator runs an ad that just lists its new tariff's price, data limit, minutes and coverage area. Which purpose of advertising does this mainly serve?
why: Everyone already knows the operator, so awareness isn't the point. The ad gives details about features and characteristics, which is the 'inform' purpose.

q: Advertising that the audience clearly knows is an ad, like a TV commercial break or the ads before a cinema film, is called:
why: He contrasts traditional advertising, where you know it's an ad, with product placement, which he also calls hidden or unnoticed advertising.

q: A real commercial product used in fictional and other media or in sports, usually without being noticed, is:
why: That's the slide definition. What makes it different from traditional advertising is that viewers usually don't notice it as an ad.

q: In a popular Uzbek TV series, the main character always drinks one clearly labelled brand of iced tea. Nobody mentions the brand and there's no ad break. What is this?
why: A real product placed inside fiction without announcing it is product placement, like the sponsors' GM, German or Toyota cars in American films. The actor gives no advice or endorsement, so it isn't an appeal to authority.

q: A sponsor's logo is printed on the chest and back of a football club's shirts. How does the lecture classify this?
why: His football example: the match isn't paused to announce an ad, the logo is just there and we take it in while watching. Traditional ads interrupt the show and are clearly ads.

q: Why does the lecture say we must evaluate advertisements critically?
choices: Businesses chasing profit sometimes use tactics that are misleading, confusing or morally wrong
Most advertising in a consumer culture is illegal and should be reported to the authorities
Advertisements almost never contain any true information about the products they sell
Consumers are legally responsible for checking every ad before they buy anything
why: In a consumer culture built on profit, some businesses cross the line into tactics that mislead people. The lecture's list of fallacies is the toolkit for spotting them.

q: An ad that makes you feel fear, insecurity or shame, or that you'll be left behind, unless you buy the product is using:
why: Scare tactics work through fear of what happens if you don't buy. Questionable cause works the other way, promising something wonderful if you do.

q: A chewing-gum ad on Uzbek TV: 'Do you know what people whisper about your breath? Don't risk it. Chew FreshOn.' Which fallacy is this?
why: It plays on fear and shame of being avoided. That's his own gum and toothpaste example: if you don't use it, people won't come near you.

q: AI-company CEOs warn in public that AI could threaten humanity within a few years. The lecturer suggests this also works as marketing. Which tactic is it, and what's the hidden message?
choices: Scare tactics; the hidden message is that their product is extremely powerful
Hyperbole; the hidden message is that AI is actually completely harmless
Inappropriate authority; the hidden message is that CEOs aren't real scientists
Euphemism; the hidden message is that the danger is smaller than it sounds
why: He calls it scare tactics: on the surface it's a warning, underneath it says 'our product can do so many things'. It isn't inappropriate authority, because they're talking about their own field.

q: An ad that creates a false expectation that using the product will make you more beautiful, thinner, more popular or happier commits:
why: The ad sets up a cause-and-effect link that isn't really there. The lecture calls it the same logic as scare tactics, but pointing at a wonderful outcome rather than a feared one.

q: A perfume ad: a shy student sprays it once, and the next day the whole faculty wants to be her friend. Which fallacy does the ad mainly rely on?
why: The perfume is shown as the cause of her new popularity, with no real causal link. Snob appeal would instead link it to people who are already glamorous or successful.

q: What separates scare tactics from questionable cause in advertising?
choices: Scare tactics threaten something bad if you don't buy; questionable cause promises something good if you do
Scare tactics rely on misleading statistics, while questionable cause relies on famous celebrities
Scare tactics exploit unclear grammar, while questionable cause exploits soft, pleasant word choices
Scare tactics are aimed only at adults, while questionable cause is aimed only at teenagers
why: Both build a false cause-and-effect link. The difference is direction: fear of a bad outcome if you don't buy, versus the promise of a wonderful one if you do.

q: An ad pushing you to buy because 'everyone already has one', which the lecture says hits teenagers and young people hardest, uses:
why: His examples are Nike shoes and iPhones among young people; the textbook even reports US cases of theft and murder over such items. Snob appeal is narrower: linking the product to attractive or successful people.

q: A payment app's billboard in Tashkent: 'Join the 5 million Uzbeks who already pay with us!' Which fallacy is this?
why: The message is 'everyone is doing it, so you should too'. Being popular doesn't make an app good or safe.

q: Which of these slogans is an example of popular appeal?
choices: 'Over 3 million families in Uzbekistan already trust our fridges'
'Our fridges are as strong as a mountain'
'The miracle fridge of the century: nothing on Earth keeps food fresher'
'Naturally fresh, because it's made from natural materials'
why: Pointing to how many people already use it is popular appeal. The others are a false analogy, hyperbole and the naturalistic fallacy.

q: Snob appeal in advertising means:
choices: Linking the product with attractive, strong or successful people and a desirable lifestyle
Claiming that nearly everyone around you, your classmates and neighbours, already owns the product
Having a famous person give expert advice on something outside their own field
Exaggerating the product with words like 'miracle' and 'must-see'
why: Snob appeal sells an image: buy this and you join the beautiful, strong, successful people. 'Everyone has it' is ordinary popular appeal.

q: How does the lecture relate snob appeal to popular appeal?
choices: Snob appeal is a type of popular appeal
Snob appeal is the opposite of popular appeal
Snob appeal is a type of scare tactic
Snob appeal is a fallacy of grammar, unrelated to popular appeal
why: He introduces snob appeal as a type of popular appeal: instead of 'everyone has it', the message is 'the beautiful, successful people have it'.

q: A beer commercial shows only good-looking, laughing young people at a rooftop party overlooking Tashkent City. Which fallacy is it mainly using?
why: It ties the drink to an attractive, fun lifestyle. That's his own example: alcohol ads showing drinkers as happier and having more fun. It doesn't claim everyone drinks it, so it isn't plain popular appeal.

q: A celebrity, athlete or scientist endorsing a product outside their own field of expertise is:
why: Experts have a narrow field. Using famous people (even scientists or politicians) to sell things they know nothing about is an appeal to inappropriate authority.

q: A famous Uzbek pop singer stars in a bank ad, explaining that this bank's deposit rates are 'the smartest financial decision you can make'. Which fallacy is this?
why: She is presented as giving financial advice, which is outside her expertise. If the ad only showed her glamorous life with the bank card and gave no advice, snob appeal would fit better.

q: Which endorsement is the clearest appeal to inappropriate authority?
choices: A champion boxer recommending a brand of baby formula
A paediatrician explaining the recommended vaccine schedule
A professional chef recommending the frying pan she cooks with
A football coach recommending a fitness-tracking app
why: A boxer has no expertise in infant nutrition. The other three speak within, or close to, their own field.

q: According to the lecture, how does hasty generalization usually show up in advertising?
choices: Ads that reinforce stereotypes about women or men
Ads that compare the product to something powerful
Ads with unclear grammar that leaves room for interpretation
Ads that hide the product inside films and sports
why: He says ads can reinforce stereotypes, e.g. that women follow certain standards or that men behave a certain way. The others are false analogy, amphiboly and product placement.

q: A washing-powder ad shows only women doing laundry and ends with: 'Every good wife knows the secret of white shirts.' Which fallacy is this?
why: It reinforces a stereotype about what women do and what makes a 'good wife', which the lecture files under hasty generalization.

q: What is amphiboly, as the lecture applies it to ads?
choices: Ambiguous grammar that allows more than one reading
Swapping harsh words for softer, less offensive ones
Exaggerating a product with words like 'miracle'
Using numbers that are true but misleading out of context
why: Amphiboly is about sentence structure, not word choice. Swapping words for softer ones is euphemism.

q: Why might a company deliberately use amphiboly, according to the lecture?
choices: If it is sued, it can argue it meant a different interpretation
Ambiguous slogans are cheaper to print and to translate
Unclear grammar frightens customers into buying quickly
It links the product to successful, attractive people
why: He says the vague grammar leaves room for interpretation, so if someone sues over the negative reading, the company can claim it meant something else.

q: A billboard reads: 'GlowCream: use it and be loved.' A customer complains that nothing changed, and the company replies that the slogan was two friendly wishes, not a promise. Which fallacy is the slogan built on?
why: The 'and' leaves it grammatically open whether the cream causes being loved, and the company uses that to dodge responsibility, like 'Wear it and be happy' from Lecture 4. A plain promise ('this cream will make you loved') would be questionable cause.

q: An online shop advertises: 'Free delivery in Tashkent and the regions on orders over 200,000 sum.' A Tashkent customer orders for 80,000 sum and is charged for delivery; the shop says the minimum applies everywhere. What's the problem with the ad?
choices: Amphiboly: the sentence can be read two ways
Euphemism: 'free' is a softer word for a fee
why: It can mean 'free in Tashkent, and free in the regions over 200,000' or 'free everywhere over 200,000'. That grammatical ambiguity, which the shop then reads in its own favour, is amphiboly.

q: The naturalistic fallacy in an ad assumes that:
choices: Whatever is natural is good or safe
Whatever is popular must be good
Whatever is expensive is high quality
Whatever is newest is better than the old
why: Natural doesn't mean safe: tobacco, earthquakes and poisonous plants are all natural. 'Popular means good' is popular appeal.

q: A herbal supplement sold on Instagram: '100% natural, so there are no side effects. Safe for everyone, even pregnant women.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The whole safety claim rests on 'natural', but natural substances can be harmful or interact with medicines. That's the naturalistic fallacy.

q: A cigarette brand advertises '100% natural tobacco, no additives'. Which fallacy does the lecturer say this commits?
why: This is his own example. Even natural tobacco harms your health, so 'natural' says nothing about safety. The persuasion rests on the word 'natural', not on exaggeration.

q: Replacing words for an unpleasant reality with softer, less scary or less offensive ones, while still leading to the same conclusion, is:
why: Euphemism is substitution of words. It's the opposite move from hyperbole, which inflates rather than softens.

q: A microloan company's ad calls its high-interest loans 'a friendly financial helping hand'. Which technique is this?
why: A costly debt gets a soft, friendly label. The product is the same; only the words are less scary.

q: A company's press release says it is 'optimising its workforce' when it is firing 300 employees. Which technique is this?
why: The lecture notes that politicians and marketers both use euphemism. 'Optimising the workforce' is a softer label for mass firing.

q: Which description matches hyperbole in ads?
choices: Exaggeration, as in 'must-see', 'product of champions' or 'miracle'
A soft word replacing a harsh one, as in 'pre-owned' for 'used'
A comparison with something powerful, as in 'strong as stone'
An ambiguous sentence, as in 'wear it and be happy'
why: These are his own hyperbole examples. The others describe euphemism, false analogy and amphiboly.

q: A plov centre's sign: 'The best plov in the universe. A must-try!' Which fallacy is this?
why: Pure exaggeration, the same pattern as his 'must-see cinema' and 'must-go place'.

q: Three of these slogans are euphemisms. Which one is hyperbole instead?
choices: 'Budget seating' for the cramped back rows
why: Hyperbole inflates; euphemism softens. 'Pre-loved' means used, 'price adjustment' means a price rise, and 'budget seating' hides cramped seats.

q: In the lecture, the 'analogy' problem in ads is:
choices: A weak comparison between the product and something powerful
Linking the product to attractive, successful people and their lifestyle
Using true numbers in a way that misleads once you see the context
Using a celebrity to give advice outside their area of expertise
why: He describes it as an inductive argument by analogy: the comparison borrows the strength of something else, and often it's weak or false.

q: A car ad says: 'Our cars are like stone.' Why does the lecturer call this a weak analogy?
choices: Stone lasts for centuries, but a car loses value within 5–10 years
Stone is natural, and natural things aren't always good
The slogan's grammar can be read in two different ways
'Stone' is a softer word that hides how heavy the car is
why: The cars share almost nothing with stone that matters to a buyer, so the comparison falls apart. The other choices describe the naturalistic fallacy, amphiboly and euphemism.

q: A watch brand's billboard near the Registan: 'Like the Registan, our watches will stand for centuries.' Which fallacy does the comparison commit?
why: It borrows the lasting strength of a 600-year-old monument through comparison, but a watch shares little with a stone madrasa. Persuasion by a weak comparison is the analogy problem.

q: What is the lecture's point about 'logic and statistics' in ads?
choices: Numbers can check out as accurate yet still mislead once you look at the context
Statistics in ads are almost always invented, so they can safely be ignored
Ads are legally banned from using statistics, so any number is a red flag
Statistics are the most trustworthy part of an ad, since numbers can't lie
why: He alludes to 'lies, damned lies and statistics': the numbers may be correct if you double-check them, but put in context, or with the math done, they can deceive.

q: A study centre advertises: '98% of our students passed the IELTS!' You later learn only 40 students sat the exam, after weaker students were told not to take it. Which issue is this?
choices: Hasty generalization from a small sample
why: The 98% may be technically true, but it hides who was counted. True-but-misleading numbers are the lecture's 'logic & statistics' problem; hasty generalization in ads, per the lecture, is about stereotypes.

q: Why does the lecture open with global warming, COVID, nuclear energy in Uzbekistan, AI and vaccines?
choices: Each has conflicting 'research'-backed narratives, so we need tools to judge them
They are examples of settled science that no longer needs any public debate at all
They show that only scientists should be allowed to comment on public issues
They are the lecture's main examples of pseudoscience in the news
why: On each topic some news and research is positive and some negative. The question 'where is the truth?' is why a critical thinker needs to understand how science works.

q: According to the lecture, science is the use of reason to move from:
choices: Observable facts to hypotheses to testable explanations
Accepted paradigms to laws that can never again be questioned
Personal experience and intuition to moral values
Expert opinion to popular agreement on what is true
why: That's the slide definition. The facts are the data; the end product is an explanation that can be tested.

q: What does the lecture describe as the task of scientists?
choices: To discover, observe and collect facts systematically and explain how they relate
To prove their explanations true with 100% certainty before publishing anything
To decide which values and beliefs society ought to hold
To replace religious explanations of the world with materialist ones
why: Systematic collection of facts, plus explaining the relationships between them. 100% proof is impossible, which is why the lecture later uses falsifiability as the test.

q: Some cultures treat science as the natural way of seeing reality. What does the lecture remind us science also is?
choices: A human-made system built on a worldview and assumptions
A method so free of assumptions that its results can never be biased
A religion with its own scriptures, rituals and authorities
A field limited to studying human societies rather than nature
why: Science is a human creation built on assumptions (empiricism, objectivity, materialism, predictability, unity), and those assumptions have limits.

q: Which five assumptions underlie science, according to the lecture?
choices: Objectivity, paradigm, normal science, revolution, unity
why: The third list is the criteria for evaluating a hypothesis, dualism is the minority alternative to materialism, and paradigm and revolution are Kuhn's terms.

q: The belief that our physical senses are the primary source of knowledge, so that more data and observations mean better explanations of nature, is:
why: Empiricism treats the empirical method, knowledge gathered from the physical world through the senses, as the only reliable way to know.

q: The assumption that we can study the physical world as an object outside us, without bias, so that systematic observation will lead scientists to agree, is:
why: Objectivity assumes the scientist stands outside what they study, which supposedly puts them in a neutral position. Kuhn later challenges this.

q: The assumption that everything in the universe is made of physical matter is:
why: Materialism is the working assumption of most scientists. Dualism adds a separate non-material, spiritual realm.

q: When the lecture calls materialism the working assumption of most scientists, what does 'materialism' mean here?
choices: Everything in the universe is physical matter
Scientists love buying and consuming things
Research is mostly paid for by businesses
Only expensive instruments give valid data
why: He stresses it's not the consumer or marketing sense of 'materialistic'. It's the claim that everything is physical, so non-physical things may be ignored.

q: The view, held by some scientists, that besides physical matter there is an independent non-material or spiritual realm is called:
why: Dualism is the minority view. Most scientists work from materialism, which says everything is physical.

q: The assumption that the universe is orderly, made of interconnected causal relationships we can discover through systematic observation and inductive reasoning, is:
why: Predictability is about orderly cause and effect. Unity, which is linked to it, is the further belief in one underlying structure in everything.

q: The assumption that there is an underlying unified, dynamic structure present in all things is:
why: Unity goes beyond predictable causes: it says one structure runs through all phenomena.

q: A scientist says: 'If something can't be seen, measured or detected by our senses or instruments, I can't count it as knowledge.' Which assumption of science is she relying on?
why: Treating the senses (and the instruments that extend them) as the source of knowledge is empiricism. Its limit: dark matter and other things our senses can't reach.

q: A physicist spends her career looking for a single 'theory of everything' that would explain all the forces of nature at once. Which assumption drives this search?
why: Believing that one underlying structure runs through all phenomena is the unity assumption. Predictability is related but narrower: orderly cause and effect.

q: Which philosopher argued that we only have an idea in our mind of a world outside us, not direct evidence that this world actually exists?
why: The lecture uses Descartes as the first limitation of science. Kuhn wrote about paradigms, Wegener proposed continental drift, and Copernicus heliocentrism.

q: The lecture mentions dark matter, dark energy, some electromagnetic waves and atomic particles to illustrate that:
choices: Empiricism limits science to what can be observed
Quantum mechanics has shown that the universe isn't orderly
Observation can never establish a necessary causal link
Science is a social construct shaped by its society
why: These may not be detectable by our senses, or by instruments built as extensions of our senses. So science based on empiricism only covers what is observable and shared.
