q: Which development has called into question the assumption that the universe is orderly and predictable?
why: The lecture names quantum mechanics as the challenge to orderliness and predictability. The Big Bang is his example of a hypothesis with strong predictive power.

q: For years a student has noticed that the bus arrives right after the corner café opens, and she concludes that the café opening makes the bus come. Which limitation of science does this illustrate?
choices: Observation alone can't establish a necessary causal connection between two events
Empiricism limits science to what is observable and shared
Quantum mechanics makes events impossible to predict
We only have an idea of the outside world in our minds, never direct evidence that it exists
why: However many times B follows A, observation by itself can't prove that A causes B. The textbook credits this point to David Hume; it undermines the predictability assumption.

q: Before telescopes and space missions, people 'saw' meaningful shapes, channels or mountains on the Moon and planets that later turned out to be something else. What does the lecture use this to show?
choices: Our brains organise and give meaning to what our senses take in
Empiricism always gives accurate knowledge if we observe long enough
Ancient astronomy was a paradigm that never needed to change
Quantum mechanics had already disproved the old view of the planets
why: Our brains bring old ideas and experiences to what we see. Better technology later showed the planets were very different from how they seemed.

q: Which position on science and religion does the lecture say most scientists and Western philosophers hold?
choices: Science always trumps religion when they conflict
Religion always trumps science when they conflict
They work in separate, mutually exclusive realms
They concern the same reality and complement each other
why: Position one. It created antagonism with fundamentalist religion, which reads scripture as the literal word of God, and helped produce the opposite camp (religion trumps science).

q: A preacher tells his followers: 'Whenever a scientific finding disagrees with our holy book, the scientists are simply wrong.' Which position is this?
why: When the two conflict, religion wins: position two. The lecture describes it partly as a reaction to the radical 'science trumps religion' camp.

q: 'Science asks how and what; religion asks why.' Which position on science and religion is this?
why: In the third position, science deals with objective, empirical reality and religion with values and subjective, spiritual reality, so they don't overlap.

q: A biology student accepts evolution, but believes the soul is given to humans in a spiritual realm that science simply doesn't deal with. Which position is she taking?
why: This is the lecture's own example of the third position: you can accept evolution without giving up your religious convictions, because ensoulment happens in the spiritual realm.

q: What problem does the lecture point out with the 'separate realms' view of science and religion?
choices: Sometimes both make claims about the same events, and conflicting claims can't both be true
It forces believers to reinterpret their scripture every time science changes its mind
It means religion must always give way to science whenever a conflict appears
It only works for scientists who already accept the dualist assumption
why: Science and scripture sometimes speak about the same historical events. When those claims clash, logically they can't both be true, so the realms aren't fully separate.

q: A theologian says: 'If a verse seems to conflict with well-established science, we should reinterpret the verse, because faith and science describe one reality from different sides.' Which position is this?
choices: Science always trumps religion in a conflict
Religion always trumps science in a conflict
why: Reinterpreting scripture when it clashes with science is the fourth position. It isn't 'science trumps religion', because the aim is for both to converge and inform each other, not to discard religion.

q: The scientific method is described as a process involving:
choices: The rigorous, systematic application of observation and experimentation
Emotional appeals and rhetoric aimed at winning public support
The accepted view of what the world is like and how to study it
The replacement of an old, problematic paradigm by a newer one
why: That's the slide definition. The others describe pseudoscience, a paradigm and a scientific revolution.

q: The lecture says the scientific method is similar to which earlier idea from the course?
choices: Kuhn's normal science, paradigm and revolution
The four positions on science and religion
why: These are the three levels of thinking from earlier in the course. Just as experience alone isn't enough without interpretation and analysis, the scientific method moves from a problem through data to tested explanations.

q: What is the correct order of the scientific method's steps?
choices: Problem → hypothesis → gather info and refine → test → evaluate
Hypothesis → problem → gather info and refine → test → evaluate
Problem → test → hypothesis → evaluate → gather info and refine
Gather info and refine → problem → hypothesis → evaluate → test
why: You need a problem before an explanation, you refine the explanation before testing it, and you evaluate only once you have results.

q: A master's student searches Google Scholar and journal databases to see what's already known about youth unemployment in Uzbekistan and where the gaps are. Which step of the scientific method is she on?
choices: Gathering information to refine the hypothesis
why: He puts the literature review in step one: it shows whether someone already solved the problem and where the gaps are. Refining comes later, once you already have a hypothesis.

q: After guessing that phone use lowers students' grades, a researcher reads more studies and books, talks to professors, and narrows her idea to 'phone use after midnight lowers exam scores'. Which step is this?
choices: Refining the hypothesis with more information
Identifying the problem and its gaps
Testing the hypothesis in a study
Evaluating the hypothesis against the results of testing
why: She already has a hypothesis and is improving it with more information, which is step three. Nothing has been tested yet.

q: A lab gives a new drug to one group of mice and nothing to another, then measures their blood sugar for a month. Which step of the scientific method is this?
why: Testing can happen in a lab, through simulation or by experiment, depending on the subject. Evaluation comes after, when the results are compared with the hypothesis.

q: After an experiment, a team compares the results with what they expected and concludes that their hypothesis was wrong, but that they found something new worth reporting. Which step is this?
why: Step five judges the hypothesis on the basis of the test results: right, wrong, or a new contribution to the field.

q: A proposed explanation for a particular set of phenomena is a:
why: A hypothesis is the initial proposed explanation (step two). It becomes part of a theory only after it has been tested and supported many times.

q: An explanation of some aspect of the natural world, based on well-substantiated facts, laws and tested hypotheses, is a:
why: A theory rests on hypotheses that have already been tested. His examples are relativity and human capital theory.

q: Human capital theory says that investing more in education leads to higher earnings later. Why does the lecturer call it a theory rather than just a hypothesis?
choices: Many researchers have tested it and a large body of data supports it
It was proposed by a well-known economist working in the USA
It is the simplest explanation, so it never needed any testing
It cannot be falsified by any observation or experiment
why: A hypothesis becomes a theory when it has been tested many times and a lot of evidence supports it. Being unfalsifiable would make it worse, not better.

q: Which five criteria does the lecture use to evaluate a hypothesis?
choices: Popular, natural, well-funded, quickly published, peer-approved
why: In full: relevant to the problem, consistent with well-established theories, simplest, testable and falsifiable, and predictive. The second list is the assumptions of science, and the third is the steps of the scientific method.

q: A student researching why IUT students skip morning classes ends up adding hypotheses about global oil prices and national GDP, because she never clearly defined her problem. Which criterion is she failing?
why: A hypothesis must relate to the phenomenon it explains. He warns that a vague, too-broad problem leads down a 'slippery path' of off-topic hypotheses and conclusions.

q: Why does the lecture advise new researchers to keep their hypotheses consistent with well-established theories?
choices: It gives them validation from the research community
It guarantees that the hypothesis will turn out to be true
It makes any hypothesis automatically testable and falsifiable
It protects them from publish-or-perish pressure at work
why: Science is a system of logically consistent hypotheses and theories. Building on tested theories lends a new study support, though it doesn't prove it right.

q: If two rival hypotheses both meet the basic criteria, which one do scientists generally accept?
why: The lecture calls this a logical principle well known among scientists (usually called Occam's razor).

q: According to the lecture, one reason most scientists reject intelligent design is that:
choices: The theory of evolution seems simpler
Intelligent design has too few followers
Intelligent design was proposed by outsiders
why: This is his example of the simplicity criterion. He adds a caveat: genuinely new ideas are often not simple and may go against well-established narratives.

q: The Big Bang theory predicted not only that the universe is expanding but also the amount of helium in it and the distribution of galaxies. Which criterion does this illustrate?
why: A good hypothesis can predict and explain similar events. The greater its predictive power, the more 'fruitful' it is, meaning it suggests new ideas for future research.

q: A researcher checks whether human capital theory, developed in the USA in the 1960s, also predicts that better-educated workers in Uzbekistan earn more. What does this show about a good theory?
choices: It can predict the outcome of similar events in a new context
Once accepted, it no longer needs to be checked against data
It only applies in the country where it was first developed
Applying it in another country turns it into pseudoscience
why: His own example of predictive power: a well-established theory lets you predict results elsewhere, and then test whether they hold.

q: Why is falsifiability, rather than confirmation, used as the test of a good scientific explanation?
choices: Nothing can be proven 100% true, but a claim can be shown false
Confirming a hypothesis is considered unethical in modern research
Falsified hypotheses are simpler and therefore always preferred
Only hypotheses that have been falsified can become new paradigms
why: No number of confirming cases gives certainty, but one counter-example can refute a claim. A good hypothesis must also be testable and replicable by other scientists.

q: The hypothesis 'all swans are white' was based on observing thousands of white swans. What happened, and what does it show?
choices: One black swan proved it false, showing the claim was falsifiable
Thousands more white swans confirmed it with 100% certainty
It was rejected for not being the simplest explanation
It became a paradigm because it had many followers
why: It took only one non-white swan to refute it, and black swans were later found. That's the lecture's example of why falsifiability, not confirmation, is the test.

q: A fortune teller says: 'Something important will happen to you this year.' Why is this not a good scientific hypothesis?
choices: Almost any outcome would fit it, so it can't be falsified
It is far too simple to count as a proper scientific hypothesis
It is inconsistent with well-established theories like human capital
It was made without the client's informed consent
why: If no possible observation could show it wrong, it fails the 'testable and falsifiable' criterion. Vague claims like this are typical of pseudoscience.

q: A body of explanations that masquerades as science to gain legitimacy, but rests on emotional appeals, superstition and rhetoric, is:
why: Science grounds its explanations in systematic observation, reason and testing. Pseudoscience only borrows its look.

q: Which group does the lecture give as examples of pseudoscience?
choices: Astrology, numerology, mind reading, psychic healing
Quantum mechanics, relativity, the Big Bang
Ethnography, grounded theory, narrative and action research
why: Heliocentrism and continental drift were once rejected but became accepted science through paradigm shifts. Ethnography and the rest are legitimate research designs.

q: A 'bioenergy healer' in Tashkent claims to cure diabetes by moving his hands over patients. He shows emotional video testimonies and refuses any controlled trial. Is this science or pseudoscience?
choices: Pseudoscience: it relies on emotional testimony, not testing
Science, because many patients say that they feel better afterwards
Science, because it has many followers and could become a paradigm
Pseudoscience, but only because it isn't taught at any university
why: What makes it pseudoscience is the method: emotion and rhetoric instead of testing. Where something is taught isn't the test, and followers alone don't make a claim scientific.

q: Which claim is the most scientific?
choices: 'Students who sleep 8 hours score higher; we'll compare two groups' sleep and exam results to check.'
'Scorpios make the best engineers, because the stars shape our talents from birth.'
'This crystal relieves exam stress because it stores positive energy from the mountains.'
'My grandfather has used this herb for 50 years and swears it cures every disease.'
why: Only the first states a testable, falsifiable hypothesis and a way to test it. The others rest on astrology, superstition and personal testimony.

q: A systematic approach to gathering and analysing information, based on established scientific procedures and techniques, is:
why: Research methodology is how scientists test their hypotheses. Its concrete forms are called research methods or research designs.

q: Research that deals with numbers and things that can be counted is ___; research that focuses on meaning and experiences, using interviews or document analysis, is ___.
why: Research designs fall into two methodologies: quantitative (numbers) and qualitative (meaning).

q: A researcher holds long interviews with 12 Uzbek labour migrants about their life in Russia and analyses the meanings in their stories. Which methodology is this?
why: Focusing on meaning and experience through interviews is qualitative. There's no counting and no second method, so it isn't quantitative or mixed.

q: A researcher first surveys 500 students, then invites 20 of them for in-depth, face-to-face interviews to understand their answers better. Which research design is this?
why: This is the lecture's example of mixed methods: surveys give quick, basic answers, so interviews add depth for a more balanced result.

q: Which research design does the lecture illustrate with intervention, simulation and lab work?
why: Experimental research actively does something (an intervention, a simulation, a lab test) and measures what happens.

q: A researcher lives in a Fergana Valley mahalla for six months, observing weddings, daily routines and customs to understand the community's culture from the inside. Which research design is this?
why: Ethnography studies a culture through immersion and observation in its natural setting. The lecture lists it among the qualitative designs that focus on meaning and experience.

q: Using existing data on 10,000 households, a researcher checks whether household income and number of children rise and fall together, without changing anything. Which research design is this?
why: Measuring how two variables are related in existing data is correlational research. An experiment would need an intervention, such as changing something for one group and comparing.

q: Which experiments from the early lectures does the lecture cite as reasons why scientists began discussing research ethics?
choices: The Milgram experiment and the Stanford Prison Experiment
The black swan and Big Bang observations
Copernicus's heliocentrism and Wegener's continental drift studies
why: Incidents like Milgram's obedience study and the Stanford Prison Experiment pushed the scientific community to talk about the ethics of research.

q: Research participants agreeing of their own free will to take part, knowing the full consequences of the study, is called:
why: Informed consent is the first data-collection issue on the slide.

q: Which ethical issues does the lecture place under data collection, rather than data reporting?
choices: Informed consent and respect for site and participants
Honest reporting, proper citation and publishing on time
Political pressure and private funding of research
why: Collection is about how data is gathered from people (and animals). Honesty, citation and timely publishing are reporting issues; funding and politics fall under the neutrality of science.

q: A psychology student stages a fake fight in the dormitory and secretly films classmates' reactions, without ever telling them it was an experiment. Which ethical principle is broken?
why: The participants never agreed to take part or knew the consequences. That's a data-collection failure.

q: A research team doing fieldwork in a village photographs worshippers inside the mosque during prayer, against the community's rules. Which ethical issue is this?
choices: Respect for the site and local norms
Honest reporting of the data that was collected
Proper citation of the sources used in the study
Publish-or-perish pressure on the research team
why: Researchers must respect the place, the people and the rules where they collect data. It's a collection issue, not a reporting one.

q: Before publishing, a researcher quietly deletes the survey responses that contradict her hypothesis. Which ethical issue is this?
why: Skewing data toward your own hypothesis, worldview or politics is dishonest reporting, a data-reporting issue.

q: A lecturer translates a Russian journal article into English and publishes it under his own name. Which ethical issue is this?
why: The lecture specifically mentions presenting a translated version of someone else's work as your own. It's plagiarism, a failure of proper citation.

q: A team discovers that a cheap filter removes arsenic from village wells, but leaves the results unpublished for three years while villagers keep drinking the water. Which obligation are they neglecting?
why: Findings that could help people shouldn't sit unpublished, because those affected keep being affected. The lecture calls timely publishing an obligation of scientists.

q: A study claiming 'we are very close to AGI' turns out to be funded by an AI company. What should a critical thinker ask first, according to the lecture?
choices: Who funded the study, and who benefits from its claims?
Was the study published quickly enough?
Did the participants give informed consent before the study?
Is the hypothesis the simplest one available?
why: This is the neutrality of science. Political pressure and private or business funding can bias research, so always check who is behind a study.

q: 'Publish or perish' refers to:
choices: Pressure to publish a quota of papers to keep your job or get promoted
A rule that findings must be published within a year or else destroyed
The way old paradigms die out once new research is published
Pseudoscientists losing their followers once real studies appear
why: It comes from KPIs and metrics at universities: publish enough to keep the job, get promoted or earn more. The lecture names it as one driver of today's ethical problems in science.

q: Imagine IUT required every lecturer to publish 10 papers a year. What does the lecture expect would happen?
choices: Stress would rise, teaching would be neglected and much of the research would be shallow
Teaching would improve, because lecturers would stay up to date with current research
Research would get deeper, because there would simply be much more of it
Lecturers would stop relying on AI, since they'd have no time to learn it
why: This is his own hypothetical. Juggling teaching with a paper quota means less attention to students and very basic science, even if the university boasts about its numbers.

q: Why does the lecturer compare Einstein's output with that of some top scientists today?
choices: Einstein published about 5–6 works a year, while some publish 50–100 today, which raises doubts about quality
Einstein published far more than anyone does today, which shows modern science has slowed down badly
Einstein published nothing until he turned 50, which shows that patience pays off in science
Einstein's 300 works prove that publishing more papers always moves science forward
why: Roughly 300 works over a 50-year career is 5–6 a year. Against 50–100 a year today, he asks whether such scientists are moving science or just playing the game.

q: What is the title of Thomas Kuhn's 1962 book discussed in the lecture?
choices: Think: Critical Thinking and Logic Skills
why: Kuhn was an American physicist and historian of science. The Logic of Scientific Discovery is Karl Popper's book, and On the Origin of Species is Darwin's.

q: Kuhn challenged the idea that:
choices: The scientific method is objective and science is steadily progressive
Science is a social construct shaped by the society that produces it
Paradigms shape what scientists see and which problems they study
Progress in science comes through crises and paradigm shifts
why: The other three are things Kuhn argued for. What he attacked was the picture of science as purely objective and moving steadily forward.

q: When Kuhn calls science a 'social construct', he means that science:
choices: Is shaped by its society's expectations and professional norms
Is invented and controlled by governments to shape what their citizens are allowed to believe
Is no more reliable than astrology or numerology, since both are just opinions in the end
Only studies social phenomena such as families and markets, never the natural world
why: Like other human enterprises, science reflects its society, and its norms decide which hypotheses count as acceptable. That isn't the same as saying it's worthless.

q: Research firmly based on past scientific achievements, which a scientific community accepts for a time as the foundation for its further work, is:
why: Normal science is what fills journals and textbooks. Its achievements supply the paradigms researchers work within.

q: For Kuhn, the accepted view of what the world is like and how we should go about studying it is a:
why: A paradigm is the shared worldview and model for research. Normal science is the research done within it.

q: According to Kuhn, a paradigm becomes part of normal science when it:
choices: Solves current problems and attracts many followers
Has been proven true with 100% certainty by repeated experiments
Is the simplest explanation available to the field
Is approved by both scientific and religious authorities
why: Both conditions are needed: success at solving problems, and enough followers. No paradigm is ever proven with certainty.

q: Kuhn argues that paradigms influence:
choices: What counts as a problem, and even what we perceive
Only how research is funded, not what actually gets studied
Only how textbooks and journal articles are formatted
Nothing at all, because good scientists are fully objective
why: A paradigm shapes both the questions and the perceptions. That's why Kuhn rejects the idea that science is purely objective.

q: The lecturer says evolution became 'normal science', and scientists of the last century did their research through it like a prism. In Kuhn's terms, evolution worked as a:
why: A paradigm is the worldview through which a field sees and studies its subject. Darwinism played that role for many scientists.

q: A paradigm shift in which a new scientific theory replaces a problematic paradigm is called:
why: This is Kuhn's third concept. Revolutions break up long periods of normal science.

q: What leads to a paradigm shift, according to Kuhn?
choices: Anomalies that persist and can't be explained by the current paradigm cause a crisis
A majority vote among the leading scientists of the field
A change in which companies fund research in that field
A new experiment that confirms the old paradigm once again
why: Progress isn't linear. When anomalies pile up, a crisis follows, the old paradigm is rejected, and a new theory takes its place.

q: Copernicus's theory that the Earth goes around the Sun replaced the Earth-centred view of the universe. In Kuhn's terms, this was:
choices: Normal science building on the past
why: A new theory replaced a problematic old paradigm. The lecture uses Copernicus as the revolution of his time.

q: Alfred Wegener's continental drift theory wasn't taken seriously at first, but 30–40 years later, as data built up, it was accepted. What does this illustrate?
choices: A paradigm shift that took decades to win acceptance
Pseudoscience finally being exposed by new geological data
Normal science building smoothly on past work
A hypothesis rejected for being too simple
why: New paradigms often meet resistance. As more research and data came in, Wegener's idea replaced the old view of fixed continents.

q: The lecture notes that Einstein was only 26 when he first published his relativity hypothesis in 1905. Which of Kuhn's ideas does this support?
choices: New paradigms attract young scientists and outsiders
Publish-or-perish pressure produces great science early in a career
Scientists always accept the simplest explanation first
Normal science is carried out mainly by young researchers
why: Kuhn says new paradigms usually attract the young and people from outside the field, because they have less invested in the old paradigm.
